author: Keith Weller/USDA
title: File:Cow female black white.jpg
description:
Holstein-Friesian milk cow
Because much of the cost of a cow is the feed and labor needed to maintain her, fewer but higher yielding cows mean lower priced milk. Dairy herd improvement ultimately benefits consumers.
That's why it's just as important to keep complete and accurate records as it is to keep the cows contented. The National Cooperative Dairy Herd Improvement Program has been tracking Bossy's milk yields since 1905.
Over the years, this program has made enormous contributions to dairy cattle breeding. ARS scientists receive the lactation records of all herds enrolled in the program and use the figures to rank the bulls that sire the nation's dairy cows and to rank the cows themselves.

The results of years and years of scientific dairying? Milk production has been trending upward for more than 25 years in the United States-from about 117,000 million pounds in 1970 to more than 150,000 million pounds in 1994-even though the number of milk cows has been reduced.

author: Mullookkaaran
title: File:Vechur Cow.jpg
description: The Vechur cow is a rare breed of Bos indicus cattle named after the village Vechoor in Kottayam district of the state of Kerala in India. With an average length of 124 cm and height of 87 cm, it is the smallest cattle breed in the world according to the Guinness Book of Records, and is valued for the larger amount of milk it produces relative to the amount of food it requires. The Vechur animals were saved from extinction due to conservation efforts by Sosamma Iype, a Professor of Animal breeding and Genetics along with a team of her students. In 1989, a conservation unit was started. A Conservation trust was formed in 1998 to continue the work with farmer participation.

title: File:Sheep lounging in the shade of a tree at Röe Castle.jpg
description: A flock of sheep (Ovis aries) lounging in the shade of a tree. The flock was kept in the enclosed area of Röe Castle ruin to keep the vegetation in check. The standing matriarch is tagged in both ears meaning that she is selected for breeding and will not be slaughtered after her first year. The rest of the flock have tags in only one ear and will be slaughtered within twelve months after their birth. Röe Castle ruin, Röe, Lysekil Municipality, Sweden. The image is stacked manually from two photos (handheld) for focus and light.

author: Mostafameraji
title: File:گوسفند Sheep 3.jpg
description: The sheep is a quadrupedal, ruminant mammal typically kept as livestock. Like all ruminants, sheep are members of the order Artiodactyla, the even-toed ungulates. Although the name "sheep" applies to many species in the genus Ovis, in everyday usage it almost always refers to Ovis aries. Numbering a little over one billion, domestic sheep are also the most numerous species of sheep. An adult female sheep is referred to as a ewe (/juː/), an intact male as a ram or occasionally a tup, a castrated male as a wether, and a younger sheep as a lamb

author: Giles Laurent
title: File:016a Desert-adapted elephant dust bathing in Damaraland Photo by Giles Laurent.jpg
description: Desert-adapted elephant dust bathing in Damaraland, Namibia. Desert-adapted elephants often dust-bathe by spraying sand or dust over their bodies with their trunks. This behavior helps protect their skin from intense sun and heat, acts as a natural insect repellent, and creates a protective layer that reduces moisture loss in the harsh desert environment. Desert-adapted elephants are the same species than African bush elephants (Loxodonta africana) but have behavior and physical adaptations for life in extreme desert environments. They are generally slimmer and slightly smaller than typical bush elephants and weighing toward the lower end of the species’ range due to limited food availability. Although African bush elephants can live 60–70 years in the wild, desert-living populations often have shorter average lifespans (40-50 years) because of the harsh conditions they live in.

author: Giles Laurent
title: File:002 Male Lion prowling in the Serengeti National Park Photo by Giles Laurent.jpg
description: Male Lion (Panthera leo) prowling in the Serengeti National Park, Tanzania. Prowling primarly consists of walking slowly low-to-the-ground with head down while fixing the target and trying to be as stealthy as possible. This action is a behavior commonly expressed by large carnivores to assess their surroundings, stalk preys, or approach with reduced detectability. In this instance, the lion was pursuing a cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) mother and her three cubs, that where close to a recent kill. Lions frequently engage in kleptoparasitism by usurping kills from smaller predators and may also attack cheetahs or their offspring to reduce interspecific competition for prey resources.

author: Andreas Weith
title: File:Endangered arctic - starving polar bear.jpg
description: In summer, some polar bears do not make the transition from their winter residence on the Svalbard islands to the dense drift ice and pack ice of the high arctic where they would find a plethora of prey. This is due to global climate change which causes the ice around the islands to melt much earlier than previously. The bears need to adapt from their proper food to a diet of detritus, small animals, bird eggs and carcasses of marine animals. Very often they suffer starvation and are doomed to die. The number of these starving animals is sadly increasing.

author: آرمین
title: File:Rabbit (red eye).JPG
description: It is genetics. There are a few different genes that can cause red eyes. The albino gene (cc) is where all the color pigment is removed. This causes the eyes to appear pink. Basically it is just a lack of color. The himalayan gene (ch) also shows red eyes. The himalayan gene is just one step about the albino gene. This gene removes all the color except at the points, nose, ears etc.
